opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the energy picture is really the key to understanding why batching matters so much. If you look at what actually costs energy on a modern chip, the arithmetic itself is incredibly cheap. A low-precision multiply-add costs on the order of a fraction of a picojoule. Moving the data to do that multiply is a completely different story. Bringing a value in from off-chip memory, from HBM or DRAM, can cost something like a thousand times more energy than the operation you're actually going to do with it. Even moving data across the chip, from one SRAM bank over to the compute units, is significantly more expensive than the math.

So if you think about running a neural network one example at a time, you're pulling all these weights in from memory, paying that big energy cost per parameter, and then you do exactly one multiply with each weight and throw it away. That's a terrible trade. You've spent something like a thousand units of energy moving the weight to do one unit of useful work.

Batching changes that ratio. If you have a batch of, say, 256 examples, you bring that weight in once and reuse it 256 times. Now the cost of moving it gets amortized across all those operations, and you get much closer to being limited by the compute rather than the memory traffic. That's really what drives a lot of accelerator design. The systolic arrays in TPUs, for example, are built around the idea that once you've got a value close to the compute, you want to pass it along and reuse it as many times as possible before it goes anywhere expensive again.

It also shows up in inference in interesting ways. For training, you naturally have big batches, so it's easier. For serving, especially autoregressive decoding, you're generating one token at a time per sequence, so you're often memory-bandwidth bound. That's why you see all these techniques, batching across many users' requests, speculative decoding, quantizing weights to lower precision so there are fewer bits to move, keeping more state on-chip. They're largely all different ways of attacking the same underlying problem: data movement costs far more than computation, so you want to do as much useful work as possible per byte you move.

And I think that's going to keep shaping hardware and model design going forward. The question isn't really "how many FLOPs can you do," it's "how efficiently can you feed those FLOPs," and batching is one of the most fundamental tools for that.

r001.rationale: It says moving data from an SRAM bank to compute is significantly more energy-intensive than the math, including multiplication.

r002.rationale: It explains that batching reuses a weight across multiple examples, amortizing the energy cost of transferring it.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about it is that the energy in these systems isn't really going into the arithmetic. People tend to assume a multiply-add is the expensive thing, but on a modern process a multiply is incredibly cheap in energy terms. What's expensive is moving data. Reading a weight out of DRAM or HBM and bringing it on-chip costs orders of magnitude more energy than doing the math on it once it's there. Even moving data across the chip through the on-chip interconnect is much more than doing a flop.

So if you think about what a model is doing during inference, you have this huge set of parameters, and for each token you want to generate, you have to touch all of those weights. If you serve one request at a time, you pay the full cost of pulling every weight in from memory, and then you do exactly one multiply-add with it. That's a terrible ratio. You've spent all this energy on the memory traffic and gotten almost no useful work out of it.

Batching is how you fix that ratio. If you bring a weight on-chip and then apply it to 64 or 256 different sequences while it's sitting there, you've amortized the expensive part across a lot of useful arithmetic. The energy per token drops dramatically, and so does the dollar cost, because the hardware is being used for what it's good at rather than sitting idle waiting on memory.

That's really the core tension in accelerator design and in serving systems. Compute throughput has grown much faster than memory bandwidth, so the gap keeps widening, and the only way to actually use all those flops is to find enough parallel work. It's also why things like systolic arrays and large on-chip SRAM matter so much. They're about keeping data local and reusing it as many times as possible before it has to go anywhere.

And there's a latency angle to it too. Batching is great for throughput, but users want responses quickly, so you're constantly balancing how long you wait to fill a batch against how much efficiency you give up by running a smaller one. A lot of the clever work in serving is about getting the efficiency of large batches without making individual users feel it. Things like speculative decoding or continuous batching are really ways of getting more useful arithmetic out of each trip through the weights. But at the bottom of all of it is that simple fact: moving bits is expensive, computing on them is cheap, so you want to move each bit once and compute on it as much as you can.

r001.rationale: It says that moving data across the on-chip interconnect costs much more energy than performing a flop, and that multiplication is cheap.

r002.rationale: It explains that a weight brought on-chip can be applied to many sequences, spreading the energy cost of fetching it across multiple examples.

astra-6.text:
A useful way to think about it is that moving data can cost more energy than doing arithmetic on it. You have these accelerators that can do enormous numbers of multiply-adds, but you need to keep them supplied with data. Fetching model weights from memory has a cost, both in energy and in time.

Batching lets you amortize that cost. If you bring in a set of weights and use it for multiple examples, you’re doing more useful computation for each byte you move. That tends to improve both utilization and energy efficiency.

The tradeoff is latency. If you’re serving an interactive application, you don’t want to wait a long time to assemble a big batch. So you’re balancing how efficiently you can run the hardware against how quickly you need to respond to an individual request.

sol-6.1.text:
A useful way to think about it is that moving data often costs much more energy than doing arithmetic on it. You can do a multiply-add fairly cheaply, but fetching the operands, particularly from off-chip memory, is considerably more expensive.

Batching lets you amortize that cost. If you bring in a set of model weights and use them for many examples, instead of fetching them again for each example, you get more useful computation out of each memory access. That’s especially important for accelerators with a lot of arithmetic capacity—you need enough reuse to keep those units busy.

Of course, there’s a latency tradeoff. For training, large batches are often fairly natural. For serving, you have to balance efficiency against how long someone waits for a response. So the goal isn’t simply to make the batch as large as possible; it’s to get good utilization and data reuse within your latency constraints.

r001.rationale: The response says data movement is often more costly than arithmetic and highlights off-chip fetching, but it does not state that movement within the accelerator chip can also consume far more energy than multiplication.

r002.rationale: It explains that batching reuses a set of model weights across many examples, avoiding a separate fetch for each example and amortizing the movement cost.
